title: History of climate change policy
article: History of climate change policy and politics

definition.text: The history of political actions, policies, controversies and activism concerning climate change.

facts.text: Formal global environmental politics began with the 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm.
The first World Climate Conference in 1979 framed climate change as a global political issue, and the IPCC was set up in 1988.
Efforts have mostly sought consensus at the UN under the UNFCCC, with the 1987 Montreal Protocol cited as a precedent that this can work.
Critics of this top-down approach propose bottom-up governance instead.
Adaptation was long seen as a distraction from mitigation and gained attention only around 2009 and 2010, after the Copenhagen summit made progress on emissions look harder.
Climate policy became increasingly polarised in the late 2000s, with the US partisan gap the widest in history in 2020.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

definition.text: A climate finance fund, created at COP27 in Egypt in 2022, that supports poorer countries for climate damage that adaptation could not prevent.

facts.text: It was agreed after three decades of negotiation on loss and damage and was seen by many as a major breakthrough.
It operates as a financial mechanism of the Paris Agreement.
Industrialised nations had blocked earlier requests for such support at previous COPs.
Its operating rules were set at COP28, with $700 million in start-up capital, administered by the World Bank.
At COP29 it was announced ready to receive contributions and to start financing projects in 2025; the US withdrew its representatives in March 2025.

definition.text: An international treaty that protects the ozone layer by phasing out the production of substances that deplete it.

facts.text: It was agreed on 16 September 1987 and entered into force on 1 January 1989.
With 198 parties it was the first universally ratified treaty in UN history and is often called the most successful international environmental agreement.
Developing countries get extra time to comply under Article 5, and a financial mechanism under Article 10 helps them.
Concentrations of the main CFCs have levelled off or fallen, and the Antarctic ozone hole is slowly recovering.
It has also benefited climate change mitigation; HCFCs, which it phases out, are very potent greenhouse gases.
It is cited as a precedent that the UN consensus approach to global problems can work.

definition.text: A 2016 amendment to the Montreal Protocol under which countries promised to cut their use of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) by more than 80% over 30 years.

facts.text: It came into force on 1 January 2019.
HFCs replaced CFCs and do not harm the ozone layer, but they are greenhouse gases with a high global warming potential.
A 2009 study calculated that a fast HFC phasedown could avoid up to 8.8 Gt CO2-eq per year of emissions by 2050.

definition.text: The fund that helps developing countries with low use of ozone-depleting substances comply with the Montreal Protocol.

facts.text: It serves countries using less than 0.3 kg of ozone-depleting substances per person a year; 147 of the 196 parties qualify.
It embodies the principle of common but differentiated responsibility to protect the global commons.
It is run by an executive committee with equal numbers of industrialised and developing countries, the first such democratically managed treaty fund.
